In cases where bacterial meningitis is caused by organisms with no significant resistance to chloramphenicol and beta-lactam antibiotics, treatment should follow national guidelines or use one of the following regimens: Chloramphenicol at 25 mg/kg administered intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV) every 6 hours, combined with ampicillin at 50 mg/kg IM or IV every 6 hours. Alternatively, chloramphenicol at 25 mg/kg IM or IV every 6 hours, combined with benzyl penicillin at 60 mg/kg (100,000 units/kg) IM or IV every 6 hours. (This is a conditional recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence.) 2. For measles, there are currently no GRC-approved recommendations. Updated guidance is in progress. Until then, the 2004 guidelines for treating measles in children may be used. 3. For septicemia, there are no GRC-approved recommendations at present. Updated guidance is being developed. First-line treatment includes fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin, gatifloxacin, ofloxacin, or perfloxacin for 7–10 days. Ciprofloxacin: 15 mg/kg per dose orally, twice daily for 7–10 days. (This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence.) If treatment response is poor, consider drug-resistant typhoid and treat with second-line antibiotics such as third-generation cephalosporins or azithromycin: Ceftriaxone (IV): 80 mg/kg per day for 5–7 days. Azithromycin: 20 mg/kg per day for 5–7 days. (This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence.) Where local data on antibiotic resistance among Salmonella isolates is available, national guidelines should be followed. (This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence.) 4. For severe acute malnutrition (SAM), children aged 6–59 months should be screened by trained community health workers using mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) and checked for bilateral pitting edema. Children with MUAC <115 mm or any degree of bilateral edema should be referred immediately to a treatment center for full assessment and management of SAM. (This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence.) 5. In primary healthcare facilities and hospitals, health workers should assess MUAC or weight-for-height/length status and check for bilateral edema in children aged 6–59 months. Children with MUAC <115 mm, weight-for-height/length less than -3 Z-scores of WHO growth standards, or bilateral edema should be admitted to a SAM management program. (This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence.) 6. Children with SAM should undergo a full clinical examination to determine the presence of medical complications and assess their appetite. Children who are clinically well, alert, and have appetite can be treated as outpatients. Children with medical complications, severe edema, poor appetite, or danger signs (e.g., inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy) should be treated as inpatients. (This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence.) 7. Children admitted with SAM can be transferred to outpatient care when medical complications, including edema, are resolving, and they are clinically well, alert, and have good appetite. Transfer decisions should not be based on achieving specific anthropometric outcomes such as MUAC or weight-for-height/length. (This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence.) 8. Children with SAM should only be discharged from treatment when: Their weight-for-height/length is ≥ -2 Z-scores, and they have had no edema for at least 2 weeks, or Their MUAC is ≥125 mm, and they have had no edema for at least 2 weeks. (This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence.) If MUAC is used to identify SAM, it should also be used to confirm nutritional recovery. Similarly, if weight-for-height is used, it should be used to confirm recovery. Percentage weight gain should not be used as a discharge criterion. (This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence.) 9. Children discharged from SAM treatment programs should be periodically monitored to prevent relapse. (This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence.) 10. Children with SAM and severe bilateral edema, even without medical complications and with appetite, should be admitted for inpatient care. (This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence.) 11. Children with SAM and complications should receive parenteral antibiotics: Benzyl penicillin: 50,000 U/kg IM/IV every 6 hours, or ampicillin: 50 mg/kg IM/IV every 6 hours for 2 days, followed by oral amoxicillin: 15 mg/kg per dose every 8 hours for 5 days. (This is a weak recommendation based on low-quality evidence.) 12. Children with uncomplicated SAM managed as outpatients should receive a course of oral antibiotics such as amoxicillin or another broad-spectrum antibiotic. (This is a conditional recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence from randomized trials and very low-quality evidence from non-randomized studies.) 13. Undernourished children without severe acute malnutrition should not routinely receive antibiotics unless they show signs of clinical infection. (This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence.) 14. Children with SAM should receive the recommended daily intake of vitamin A (approximately 5000 IU) as part of therapeutic foods or a multi-micronutrient formulation. High-dose vitamin A supplementation is not required if they are receiving fortified therapeutic foods (F75, F100, or RUTF) or other daily supplements containing adequate vitamin A. (This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence.) 15. Children with SAM and diarrhea should be managed with therapeutic feeding approaches, including ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF), regardless of whether they are inpatients or outpatients. (This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence.) 16. In inpatient settings, children stabilized on F75 should transition to RUTF over 2–3 days as tolerated, with an energy intake of 100–135 kcal/kg per day. If RUTF is not accepted, F75 can be used temporarily, and the transition retried after 1–2 days. (This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence.) 17. Children with SAM and some dehydration or severe dehydration (but not in shock) should be rehydrated slowly using ORS for malnourished children (ReSoMal) orally or via nasogastric tube at 5–10 mL/kg per hour for up to 12 hours. Standard WHO low-osmolarity ORS should not be used for rehydration in children with SAM. (This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence.) 18. Children with SAM and signs of shock or severe dehydration who cannot be rehydrated orally or via nasogastric tube should receive intravenous fluids: Half-strength Darrow’s solution with 5% dextrose, or Ringer’s lactate solution with 5% dextrose. (This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence.) 19. HIV-infected children with SAM who qualify for lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) should start ART as soon as possible after stabilization of metabolic complications and sepsis, indicated by return of appetite and resolution of severe edema. ART regimens and doses should be the same as for HIV-infected children without SAM. Close monitoring is required during the first 6–8 weeks of ART initiation to identify early complications and opportunistic infections. (This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence.) 20. HIV-infected children with SAM should be managed with the same therapeutic feeding approaches as HIV-uninfected children with SAM. (This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence.) 21. Infants under 6 months of age with SAM and complicating factors (e.g., medical complications, recent weight loss, ineffective feeding, or pitting edema) should be admitted for inpatient care. Feeding should be directly observed for 15–20 minutes to assess attachment, positioning, and suckling. (This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence.)
